q: Platinum time goal, real fix, and order of XABCs vs board?
a: Platinum 10; surgery; XABCs first, board later
10 minutes; surgery is the real fix; XABCs first board later
Platinum 10 / surgery / XABCs before board
Platinum 10; surgery; XABCs first
why: Surgery is the real fix. Platinum 10 minutes. XABCs first. Board later.

q: What makes the chest box, and does an upper-belly stab still get a chest seal?
a: ribs + spine + diaphragm; yes — diaphragm position unknown
box = ribs + spine + diaphragm; yes still seal upper-belly stab
ribs, spine, diaphragm; yes chest seal (don’t know where diaphragm was)
ribs + spine + diaphragm; yes still gets a chest seal
why: Box = ribs + spine + diaphragm. Upper-belly stab still gets a chest seal. You do not know where the diaphragm was.

q: Adults vs kids breathing muscles, and what runs under each rib?
a: adults diaphragm + intercostals; kids almost all diaphragm; under rib nerve/vein/artery
adults both; kids almost all diaphragm; nerve, vein, artery under each rib
adults diaphragm+intercostals, kids almost all diaphragm; nerve vein artery under rib
adults diaphragm + intercostals; kids almost all diaphragm; nerve, vein, artery
why: Adults breathe with diaphragm + intercostals. Kids are almost all diaphragm. Under each rib: nerve, vein, artery.

q: Parietal vs visceral pleura; pneumothorax vs hemothorax; what is the mediastinum?
a: parietal=chest wall lining; visceral=on lung; pneumo=air; hemo=blood; mediastinum=middle space heart/aorta/vena cava/trachea/esophagus
parietal chest wall, visceral on lung; air vs blood in gap; middle space with heart aorta vena cava trachea esophagus
parietal wall / visceral lung; pneumo air hemo blood; mediastinum middle space
parietal=chest wall; visceral=lung lining; pneumothorax air; hemothorax blood; mediastinum middle space
why: Parietal pleura = lining of the chest wall. Visceral pleura = lining on the lung. Pneumothorax = air in that gap. Hemothorax = blood in that gap. Mediastinum = middle space: heart, aorta, vena cava, trachea, esophagus.

q: Phrenic levels; cord cut above C5 vs below C5 — breathing?
a: C3-4-5; above C5 no breathe; below C5 diaphragm works intercostals don’t
phrenic C3-4-5; above C5 they do not breathe; below C5 diaphragm still works, intercostals do not
C3, C4, C5; cut above C5 → no breathe; below C5 diaphragm works, intercostals don’t
C3-4-5 keeps diaphragm; above C5 no breathe; below C5 diaphragm yes intercostals no
why: Phrenic nerve = C3, C4, C5. Cord cut above C5 → they do not breathe. Below C5 → diaphragm still works, intercostals do not.

q: Ventilation vs respiration vs oxygenation; crackles mean fluid where?
a: vent=air in/out; resp=gas exchange; ox=O2 onto red cells; crackles=fluid in alveoli
ventilation air in/out; respiration alveoli gas exchange; oxygenation onto red cells; crackles fluid in alveoli
air in/out; gas exchange; oxygen onto red cells; crackles = fluid in the alveoli
vent in/out; resp gas exchange; ox onto red cells; crackles water or blood in alveoli
why: Ventilation: air in and out. Respiration: gas exchange in the alveoli. Oxygenation: oxygen onto red cells. Crackles = fluid in the alveoli (water or blood).

q: BVM pressure type, and where can some air go?
a: positive pressure; some air to the stomach
BVM positive pressure → some air also to stomach
positive pressure; air can go to stomach
positive pressure, some air to stomach
why: A BVM pushes air in (positive pressure), so some air also goes to the stomach.

q: Hemoptysis vs hematemesis; pink frothy sputum means what?
a: hemoptysis coughing blood=lung; hematemesis vomiting blood=gut; pink frothy=pulmonary edema
coughing blood=lung; vomiting blood=gut; pink frothy=pulmonary edema
hemoptysis=lung; hematemesis=gut; pink frothy sputum=pulmonary edema
cough blood lung; vomit blood gut; pink frothy pulmonary edema
why: Hemoptysis = coughing blood = lung. Hematemesis = vomiting blood = gut. Pink frothy sputum = pulmonary edema.

q: Paradoxical motion: one segment or whole side? Default trauma shock then what?
a: one flail segment wrong way (not whole side); default bleed then tension/tamponade
one segment (flail), not whole side; bleed first, then obstructive tension or tamponade
paradoxical = one segment flail not whole side; default bleed then tension pneumo or tamponade
one segment not whole side; bleed then tension/tamponade
why: Paradoxical motion = one segment moves the wrong way. Flail. Not the whole side. Default shock in trauma is bleed. Then think obstructive: tension pneumo or tamponade.

q: Open chest hole: what seal, how many sides, clog fix, both holes?
a: occlusive/chest seal/3-sided or non-porous; peel vent reseal if clog; seal both holes
plastic occlusive / chest seal / 3-sided; clog→peel vent reseal; in-and-out seal both
occlusive chest seal 3-sided or non-porous; peel/vent/reseal; seal both holes
occlusive / chest seal / 3-sided; peel vent reseal; both holes
why: Seal with plastic: occlusive dressing, chest seal, or non-porous dressing. Tape 3 sides or vented seal. If it clogs: peel it, let it vent, reseal. In-and-out wound: seal both holes.

q: Tension signs: shock + JVD + quiet side — trachea which way? Do we needle?
a: trachea AWAY from bad side; we do not needle (medic needle closed tension only)
trachea pushed away from bad side; we don’t needle
away from bad side; paramedic needle closed tension only — we do not needle
trachea away; we do not needle
why: Trachea pushed AWAY from the bad side. Paramedic needle is for a CLOSED tension pneumo. We do not needle.

q: Quiet one lung: fat neck veins vs flat neck veins — which injury each?
a: fat/JVD = tension; flat = hemothorax
JVD/fat veins = tension pneumo; flat/collapsed = hemo
fat veins tension; flat veins hemothorax
fat / JVD = tension; flat = hemo (bled out)
why: Neck veins fat / JVD → tension pneumo. Neck veins flat / collapsed → hemothorax.

q: Beck’s triad for tamponade; how do lungs compare to tension?
a: JVD + muffled heart + narrow pulse pressure; two good lungs (not quiet side)
JVD, muffled/quiet heart sounds, narrow PP; two good lungs → heart not lung
Beck’s: JVD, muffled sounds, narrow pulse pressure; tamponade has two good lungs
JVD muffled narrow PP; two good lungs unlike tension
why: Beck’s triad: JVD; muffled / quiet heart sounds; narrow pulse pressure. Tamponade does not have a quiet lung. Two good lungs → think heart, not lung.

q: Flail chest care — bulky dressing / sandbags?
a: no bulky dress or sandbags (old answer); ABCs O2 shock go
do not bulky-dress or sandbags; ABCs, oxygen, shock care, go
refuse bulky dressing/sandbags; ABCs oxygen shock go
no bulky dress/sandbags; ABCs O2 shock go; watch bruised lung
why: Do not tape a bulky dressing over it. Do not use sandbags. That is the old answer. ABCs, oxygen, shock care, go.

q: Pulmonary contusion: crackles timing, CPAP, BVM rule?
a: crackles hours/days; no CPAP trauma; BVM only if not breathing well
crackles can take hours may kill days later; no CPAP; BVM if not breathing well
hours to days; refuse CPAP in trauma; BVM only if not breathing well
crackles hours/days later; no CPAP; BVM if needed
why: Pulmonary contusion: crackles; can take hours; may kill days later. No CPAP in trauma. BVM only if they are not breathing well.

q: Steering-wheel hit + shock + irregular pulse; sternal and clavicle worry?
a: cardiac contusion; heart 2 inches behind sternum; clavicle can poke lung
bruised heart / cardiac contusion; sternal = heart behind it; clavicle can poke top of lung
cardiac/myocardial contusion; heart behind sternum; clavicle can poke lung
cardiac contusion; sternal→heart; clavicle can poke lung
why: Steering wheel + shock + irregular pulse = cardiac contusion. Sternal fracture: the heart is two inches behind it. Clavicle can poke the top of the lung.

q: Traumatic asphyxia look — face/neck, eyes, veins?
a: purple/bruised face and neck; bloodshot eyes; JVD
purple bruised face/neck, bloodshot whites of eyes, JVD
purple face and neck; bloodshot eyes; JVD
purple/bruised face neck + bloodshot eyes + JVD
why: Purple / bruised face and neck. Bloodshot whites of the eyes. JVD.

q: Kid drops after a ball to the chest — what happened and what do you do?
a: commotio cordis → V-fib; CPR + AED
commotio cordis (blow during recharge); CPR and AED
commotio → V-fib; start CPR + AED fast
commotio cordis; CPR + AED
why: Kid drops after a ball to the chest = commotio cordis. They drop in V-fib. CPR + AED.

q: Commotio on the EKG: normal beat order, and which wave is the hit?
a: P → QRS → T; hit during T wave (repolarization / recharge)
P QRS T; hit on T wave recharge/repolarization → V-fib
normal P→QRS→T; blow during T wave while recharging → V-fib
P→QRS→T; T-wave hit (repolarization)
why: Normal beat: P wave → QRS → T wave. The hit is during the T wave — recharge / repolarization. Force fire while recharging → V-fib.

q: Pulse pressure: Cushing/ICP vs tamponade — example numbers?

wide Cushing 200/90; narrow tamponade
why: Head / Cushing / ICP: high and WIDE. Example 200/90. Cardiac tamponade: NARROW and low.

q: Can you pinch the chest aorta like a limb? Torn aorta / aneurysm / mesh sleeve?
a: no access unless chest open; torn often dead on scene; aneurysm tearing pain; mesh sleeve ≠ bypass graft
limb yes chest aorta no; torn often dead on scene; medical aneurysm tearing chest pain; sleeve ≠ graft
cannot pinch chest aorta; trauma tear often dead on scene; aneurysm tearing pain; mesh ≠ bypass
no chest aorta pinch; often dead on scene; tearing chest pain; mesh sleeve not bypass graft
why: We have no access to the chest aorta unless already wide open. Torn aorta often dead on scene. Medical aneurysm: tearing chest pain. Mesh sleeve / sock is not a bypass graft.
